gloss_terse: to cleave, split, pierce; in Piel to cut open or through, slice into
gloss_readable: A verb denoting the forceful action of splitting or cleaving. In its Qal form it describes ploughing or splitting the earth (Ps 141:7), while the Piel intensifies the image to piercing through organs (Job 16:13; Prov 7:23) or slicing produce into a pot (2 Kgs 4:39). The Spanish 'atraviesa' (pierces through) and 'dan-a-luz' (give birth) capture the range from violent penetration to the parting open in childbirth (Job 39:3). The root shares cognates with Arabic and Aramaic words for cleaving and tilling.

senses.1: To cleave, split open, or pierce with force. Covers ploughing earth (Ps 141:7), piercing kidneys and liver as figures of devastating attack (Job 16:13; Prov 7:23), slicing gourds into a pot (2 Kgs 4:39), and possibly the bursting open of the womb in birth (Job 39:3). Spanish 'atraviesa' and English 'He-pierces' reflect the violent directional thrust, while 'one-splitting' and 'el-que-ara' show the agricultural application.

gloss_terse: Pelatiah — personal name meaning 'Yah has delivered,' borne by several OT figures
gloss_readable: A theophoric name compounded from the root p-l-t (deliver, rescue) with the divine suffix -yahu/-yah, meaning 'Yahweh has delivered.' It is borne by at least three individuals: a prince of the people whose sudden death Ezekiel witnessed in a vision (Ezek 11:1, 13), a grandson of Zerubbabel in the Davidic line (1 Chr 3:21), and a Simeonite captain (1 Chr 4:42). The name also appears among the signatories of Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:22).

senses.1: A proper masculine name meaning 'Yahweh has delivered.' Borne by multiple figures: a civic prince in Ezekiel's vision who dies as a sign of judgment (Ezek 11:1, 13), a post-exilic descendant of Zerubbabel (1 Chr 3:21), a Simeonite leader in Hezekiah's era (1 Chr 4:42), and a covenant signer (Neh 10:22). Transliterations across languages are consistent — Spanish 'Pelatías,' English 'Pelatiah' — reflecting its well-established identity.

gloss_terse: fugitives, escapees; those who have survived destruction or exile
gloss_readable: The plural of an adjective-noun from the root p-l-t (escape), designating those who have fled or survived catastrophe. In Numbers 21:29 it describes Moab's sons given as fugitives to Chemosh. The prophetic texts use it for survivors of Babylon's fall who carry news back to Zion (Jer 50:28; 51:50) and for the remnant of Judah who fled to Egypt (Jer 44:14). Isaiah 66:19 envisions these escapees as emissaries sent to distant nations.

senses.1: Fugitives or escapees — those who survive a military or divine catastrophe. Spanish renders both 'fugitivos' and 'sobrevivientes,' capturing the dual nuance of flight and survival. Applied to Moabite captives (Num 21:29), Judean refugees in Egypt from whom scarcely any will return (Jer 44:14), survivors of Babylon's destruction bearing witness to Zion (Jer 50:28; 51:50), and eschatological messengers to the nations (Isa 66:19).

gloss_terse: to roll oneself (in dust or ashes) as a mourning rite; to wallow in grief
gloss_readable: A Hithpael verb describing the act of rolling oneself in dust or ashes as an expression of intense grief or lamentation. The prophets command this ritual mourning: Jeremiah urges the daughter of his people to wallow in ashes (Jer 6:26) and the shepherds of the flock to do likewise (Jer 25:34). Ezekiel depicts Tyre's mariners casting dust and rolling in ashes in anguish (Ezek 27:30). Micah 1:10 uses it in a wordplay on the city of Beth-le-aphrah ('house of dust').

senses.1: To roll oneself in dust or ashes as a mourning ritual, expressing profound grief or humiliation. Spanish 'revuélcate' (roll yourself) captures the reflexive, physical act. Commanded as prophetic mourning (Jer 6:26; 25:34), performed by Tyre's sailors in lamentation (Ezek 27:30), and employed in a place-name wordplay at Micah 1:10. The Hithpael stem emphasizes the self-directed, deliberate nature of this ritual act of abasement.

gloss_terse: flat (of hand/foot); used in 'ketonet passim,' an ornamental long-sleeved tunic
gloss_readable: A noun meaning the flat of the hand or sole of the foot, appearing exclusively in the construct phrase ketonet passim — the famous garment reaching to the palms and soles. Jacob gave such a tunic to Joseph (Gen 37:3, 23, 32), and Tamar wore one as a royal princess (2 Sam 13:18-19). The traditional rendering 'coat of many colors' follows the LXX, but the Hebrew points to an ankle-and-wrist-length robe signifying special status. Multilingual glosses reflect the interpretive tradition: German 'bunt' (colorful), Spanish 'colores.'

senses.1: The flat of the hand or sole of the foot, used exclusively in the phrase ketonet passim to describe a tunic extending to the extremities — a garment of distinction. Given by Jacob to Joseph as a mark of favor (Gen 37:3, 23, 32) and worn by virgin princesses (2 Sam 13:18-19). The widespread rendering 'many colors' (English, Spanish 'colores,' German 'bunt') reflects ancient versional tradition, but the Hebrew etymology points to length and coverage rather than coloration.

gloss_terse: Peor — a mountain in Moab and the deity associated with its cult site
gloss_readable: A proper noun with two referents: a mountain in Moab overlooking the wasteland, where Balak brought Balaam for his final oracle (Num 23:28), and the deity worshiped at that site, whose cult ensnared Israel in apostasy at Shittim (Num 25:18; 31:16). The 'incident of Peor' became a byword for idolatrous seduction, recalled as late as Joshua 22:17 as a warning against unfaithfulness. The name is likely related to a root meaning 'to open wide.'

senses.1: A mountain in Moab and its associated deity. As a geographic name, it designates the height where Balaam delivered his oracle overlooking the desert (Num 23:28). As a divine name, it refers to the Moabite/Midianite god whose worship led to Israel's catastrophic apostasy (Num 25:18; 31:16), an event recalled as a cautionary precedent (Josh 22:17). Transliterations are uniform across languages — 'Peor' in English, Spanish, French, and German — reflecting its well-known place in biblical narrative.

gloss_terse: to thrust, impel, stir; in Niphal/Hithpael, to be troubled or agitated in spirit
gloss_readable: A verb whose Qal sense means to thrust or impel — used of the Spirit of Yahweh beginning to stir Samson (Judg 13:25). In the Niphal and Hithpael, the meaning shifts to inner disturbance: Pharaoh's spirit was troubled after his dreams (Gen 41:8), and Nebuchadnezzar's spirit was agitated so that sleep fled (Dan 2:1, 3). The psalmist uses the Niphal to express deep personal turmoil (Ps 77:4). Spanish 'se turbó' and German 'beunruhigt' both capture this restless anxiety.

senses.1: To thrust, impel, or stir — and in reflexive/passive stems, to be deeply troubled or agitated in spirit. The Qal describes divine impulsion of Samson by the Spirit (Judg 13:25). The Niphal/Hithpael express psychological disturbance: Pharaoh's troubled spirit after dreams (Gen 41:8), Nebuchadnezzar's agitated sleeplessness (Dan 2:1, 3), and the psalmist's restless anguish (Ps 77:4). French 'tressaillir' (to start, tremble) and Spanish 'turbado' reflect the involuntary, shaking quality of this inner upheaval.

gloss_terse: Pirathonite — a gentilicof Pirathon, a town in Ephraim
gloss_readable: A gentilic adjective identifying someone from Pirathon, a town in the hill country of Ephraim. It is applied to Abdon son of Hillel, who judged Israel and was buried at Pirathon (Judg 12:13, 15), and to Benaiah, one of David's mighty warriors and a monthly divisional commander (2 Sam 23:30; 1 Chr 11:31; 27:14). The slight spelling variation between the Samuel and Chronicles forms reflects normal scribal orthographic fluidity.

senses.1: A gentilic adjective denoting origin from Pirathon in Ephraim. Applied to the judge Abdon son of Hillel (Judg 12:13, 15) and to Benaiah among David's elite warriors (2 Sam 23:30; 1 Chr 11:31; 27:14). English, Spanish ('piratonita'), and French consistently transliterate the term. The minor spelling difference between 2 Samuel's פִּרְעָתֹנִי and the Chronicles form פִּרְעָתוֹנִי is a standard orthographic variant with no semantic distinction.

gloss_terse: horse, steed; war-horses or mounted cavalry, a less common synonym of sus
gloss_readable: A noun for horse or steed, functioning as a less frequent synonym of the common sus. It appears in military and commercial contexts: steeds traded from Togarmah alongside horses and mules (Ezek 27:14), cavalry that a king will conscript (1 Sam 8:11), horses whose swiftness is compared to a locust army (Joel 2:4), and mounted warriors in battle array (Jer 46:4; Isa 28:28). The root has cognates in Arabic, Ethiopic, and Sabaic, all meaning horse.

senses.1: Horses or steeds, especially in military and commercial settings. A less common synonym of sus, with cognates across Semitic languages (Arabic faras, Ethiopic). Used for traded steeds from Togarmah (Ezek 27:14), royal cavalry a king will draft (1 Sam 8:11), horses swift as locusts in Joel's apocalyptic vision (Joel 2:4), and mounted warriors in battle (Jer 46:4). Spanish 'jinetes' (horsemen) and French 'cavalier' show how translators sometimes render the animal by its rider, reflecting the military context.

gloss_terse: to twist, wrestle; in Niphal/Hithpael, to be tortuous, deal crookedly or shrewdly
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to twist, with both physical and moral applications. Rachel's declaration 'I have wrestled' (Gen 30:8) uses the Niphal for intense personal struggle. In wisdom literature, the Niphal participle describes the tortuous or crooked — plans of the devious (Job 5:13) and speech that is twisted and perverse (Prov 8:8). The Hithpael in the psalms expresses God's reciprocal response: 'with the crooked you show yourself shrewd' (Ps 18:26; 2 Sam 22:27), matching crookedness with inscrutable wisdom.

senses.1: To twist, wrestle, or deal tortuously. In the Niphal, it denotes wrestling or struggle (Gen 30:8, Rachel's naming of Naphtali) and moral crookedness — the 'twisted' counsel of the devious (Job 5:13) and speech that is 'tortuous and twisted' (Prov 8:8). In the Hithpael, it describes God's reciprocal dealings: with the crooked He shows Himself shrewd (Ps 18:26; 2 Sam 22:27). Spanish 'sagaz' (shrewd) and French 'pervers' capture the moral-intellectual duality — cunning that can be either wicked or divinely wise.
